inline.s: The others, longing home, each went their way; / Changchun, loving the master, hurried to stay.

blocks.text: 14. Testing the Ordinary Mind, Reprimands Repeatedly Given; Following the Master's Will, He Holds Constant Refuge

inline.s: To rid one’s evil is to loose a tangled skein; / The spirit-mind will find its hour and be free again;
But if one misapplies a little of one’s might, / For myriad aeons and a thousand births, no end in sight.

Now Ma Danyang called Qiu Changchun back and said, "The master and the elder Dharma-brothers have all changed into Taoist robes, and only then may they travel far. As you are, you are still dressed in a layman's clothes — how can you go? I have a patched robe and a Taoist cap; put them on and you can go!" Qiu Changchun was overjoyed at the words, and at once put on the patched robe and the Taoist cap, and taking up Ma Danyang's rush cushion, travel-spade, and rock-gourd all together, he set out after the master. After walking a while, he saw far off Tan, Hao, and the others following the master as they strolled. Changchun saw that in the countryside some folk were at breakfast, and thought to himself, "We set out early and have not eaten. Better that I go beg some alms to offer the master." He had never begged alms before and did not know how to do it. He hardened his face and stood at the door of a house, holding his rock-gourd in his hand. A yellow dog barked, and someone came out to look. Turning back inside, they brought a full bowl of millet rice and poured it into his gourd. Changchun, overjoyed, begged at two more houses. When the gourd was full, he carried it with both hands and hurried up to the master.

Now Master Chongyang walked a good while and stopped to rest under a great tree. He asked Liu, Hao, and the others, "Have you brought any travel money?" Liu Changsheng answered, "Because the master set out so hastily, we chased after and had not the time to ask Brother Ma for traveling money." The master said, "Since you have brought no travel money, each of you may go beg a meal; I will wait here." At these words the four each took their rock-gourds and went begging. Master Chongyang sat alone under the tree, when he saw Qiu Changchun come carrying a gourd of rice to offer the master. Master Chongyang said angrily, "Who told you to come and trouble me? I cannot accept this offering of yours!" Changchun pleaded again and again, but the master paid him no heed. Presently Liu, Hao, and the others each brought back some alms and asked the master to eat; the master ate a little of what Liu Changsheng had begged and then would take no more. When they had all finished eating, they rose together. They traveled on more than ten li, and as the light was fading they saw a cold temple by the roadside, and went in. They swept it clean, laid down their rush cushions, and sat in meditation the night through.

The next day the six, master and disciples, went on again. Qiu Changchun, following behind, begged alms along the road. When he met a good man of a house who called him in to eat, Changchun said, "I have my master ahead; he is old and has not eaten. How dare I enjoy it myself?" The good man said, "That is no trouble; go and eat, and I will prepare some clean vegetarian fare for you and fill your gourd, that you may carry it to him in time." Seeing the sense in this, Changchun went up to the table and ate his fill. Then he came down and thanked the good man, and indeed found the gourd filled with vegetarian fare; carrying it with both hands he hurried ahead. Seeing the master not far off, he only called, "Master, go slowly! Your disciple has brought your meal." Master Chongyang pretended not to hear and went straight on. Changchun took great strides to catch up and offered the food. The master looked at it and said, "This is the food of a single house; I have no merit to receive it. Have you not heard — one gourd of the food of a thousand houses, a lone body traveling ten thousand li?" Hearing the master's words, Changchun fell silent. In the twinkling of an eye the master had gone on ahead.

He thought of returning the food to the good man, but going and coming would cost him the road. He thought of eating it himself, but his belly was already full. With no recourse, he shouldered the gourd and came on behind. His two arms were numb and his whole body streaming with sweat, when he at last saw the elder Dharma-brothers seated with the master on a rock ahead, partaking of alms. Fortunately what they had begged was very little, so he straightway set this gourd of rice before them. Each took a little, and only so did they finish it. That night they lodged again in an old temple. Changchun thought to himself, "My master is a man of Shaanxi; he does not care much for rice, but loves steamed buns and noodles. Tomorrow I will beg a few buns to offer him."

That night his resolve was fixed, and the next day he indeed begged several white-flour steamed buns to offer the master. Master Chongyang said angrily, "I told you from the first I would not eat what you bring. Why do you plague me so?" So saying, he snatched the gourd and flung it to the ground, nearly cracking it. The steamed buns rolled down the slope, and Qiu Changchun hastened to pick up the gourd and gathered the buns back into it. When he looked, the master had gone far, and he straightway hurried after.

Reader, do you ask why Master Chongyang treated Changchun so insultingly? Because he had begun to study the Way in his youth, and was not like Liu, Hao, Wang, and Tan, who had already transformed their natures. Unless he was deeply polished, how could he be made into a vessel? This is exactly what is meant by grinding his disposition. Who would have known that Changchun, with a deep root and firm foundation, suffered rebuke time and again without the least resentment?

Master Wang Chongyang and his disciples, the several of them, traveled more than two months. At that time the weather was cold, and in the countryside they had begged a few bundles of firewood and straw. That night it rained and snowed, bitterly cold, so they took some of the kindling and lit a fire to warm themselves. The instant Master Chongyang saw it he grew angry within, and flung all those bundles of firewood into the fire. All at once it blazed up in towering flame, its sparks flying wildly. Master Chongyang, taking his travel-spade, pressed the firewood down a few times; the flame died at once, thick smoke billowed, and it choked them until they had nowhere to turn. The temple was small, and the wind blew inward, so Qiu and Liu and the rest, unable to bear the smoke, had no choice but to go out the gate to escape it. Each rubbing his brows and eyes, they all said, "What a choking smoke! What a choking smoke!" When the master saw they had gone out, he shut the gate, moved his rush cushion before the door, and sat with his back to it as a bar. They stood outside for a while, and the smoke no longer choked them, but then the cold seized them. They turned to push the door — how could it budge? Not daring to call out, they sat all together under the eaves. Suddenly a gust of snowy wind came, and the cold set the several of them shivering. Liu Changsheng said, "The master has taught us the fire exercise; why should we not all do it, to ward off the severer cold?"

Changchun and his fellow practitioners set to their work, closing the breath, gathering the qi, and moving it about. Before long they not only were not cold, but began to feel warm. After a while the sky grew bright, and seeing the temple gate open, they all went in. There was the master sitting on his rush cushion, his anger unabated, and he said to them, "You fear heat and dread cold; you cling to life and dread death. You abandon the true and seek the false, greedy to warm yourselves at a false fire, unwilling to turn the true fire. You crave only ease, and will not apply deep practice. With such sloth, how can you cultivate the Way to completion? If I do not chastise you heavily, in the end it will be diligence at first and sloth at the last." Then he ordered Wang Yuyang to bring the ruler, and every one of them was to be struck twenty times, to warn them for the future. Liu, Hao, and the others, hearing this, turned the color of clay and dared not reply. Qiu Changchun knelt before the master and said, "The fault is this disciple's alone; it has nothing to do with the elder Dharma-brothers. I am willing to take the punishment, and beg the master to spare them." The master said, "Since you are willing to bear it for them — at twenty each, the sum is one hundred strokes." Liu, Hao, and the others all came and begged for mercy. The master sighed, "You beg each other off — how could I not release you? But never again do this, lest you ruin your own prospects." So saying, he flung the ruler to the ground, and said to Liu Changsheng, "In a moment's impulse I resolved obstinately to wander south. Now that the interest is spent, I would still return north. Set out at once; let there be no hesitation."

So saying, he turned to go out. Qiu, Liu, and the others hurriedly rolled up their cushions, took up their spades, took leave of the old man who kept the shrine's incense, and then followed the master, taking the same road back to Shandong. Before long they reached the county of Ninghai and came to Ma Family Estate. Qiu Changchun first went in to tell Ma Danyang, and Danyang hurried out to welcome the master inside, where he lodged once more in the thatched hut behind. For a time there was nothing of note; no need to tell of it in detail.

After more than a month the disciples, hearing the master had returned, one by one came again to study the Way, and it grew lively once more. The master thought of a clever plan to send them away. How did he do it? Listen to the next chapter for the answer.
Unless the false intent be sent away, / How will the true heart come and wake the Way?

blocks.text: 15. Signifying Ascension, the Master Retires; Escorting the Coffin, the Disciples Labor

inline.s: Where the wind-stirred banner flutters, nought is true; / The pure bright nature is the Dharma-body too;
He who perceives the flower and the smile’s clear sense, / Finds not thereafter where a speck of dust may rest.

Now Master Chongyang saw that the seekers of the Way had again gathered. Examining them, he found none who truly turned his heart to the Way; they only clung to an empty fame, using the Way as a pretext, and wishing people to know they were cultivating and waking, though in truth there was not a single thought of the Way in them. If he did not make them scatter, in time the false would confound the true, and the Dharma-gate could not be kept pure.

He thought of a clever plan, nodded his head, and suddenly called out loudly, "It is bad! It is bad!" Astounded, the people all crowded round to ask the reason. The master said, "I should not have gone out. On the road I took in the summer's heat and damp, so that my heart grew congested and blisters rose on my body." He opened his robe and showed them, and indeed his heart was swollen and his whole body covered in blisters. Alarmed, Ma Danyang and Qiu and Liu all hastened to find a physician and a cure. They invited one famous doctor after another, used several doses of wonderful medicine, but none did the least good. After two more days the blisters festered and broke, with pus and blood flowing and a stench hard to bear. Those who had come to study the Way and cultivate said secretly among themselves, "Master Chongyang surely has no Way. One who cannot protect himself, how can he save others? He cannot even be rid of an illness — how can he become an immortal? We had best go back, each of us, lest we waste our time on a lost cause." Thereupon, one slipping away quietly, another openly, in less than two days they were gone clean, leaving only Qiu, Liu, Tan, Ma, Hao, and Wang — the six — to attend him day and night.

When the master saw that the crowd had all gone, he called the six of them near and directed them, "At noon tomorrow I will surely die. But since I came here, the silver in Ma Yu's household I used to succor the poor and needy, and to help others with burials and weddings, and to give serving-girls away in marriage, and to finish the trousseaus and betrothal-gifts for the young men of the household — a good deal of silver was spent. And I supported those who came to study the Way for a year or two, and so the silver was all used up. Now the storehouse is empty. When I die, if a funeral is to be held, land must be pledged and sold. But follow my instruction and spend no money. When I die, you need not grieve and wail, and there is no need for offerings and mourning-visits. Only take a few thin boards to contain this stinking skin-bag, and let the five of you, Qiu, Liu, Wang, Tan, and Hao, carry it back in turn to Chū (
chū

) county of Shaanxi, beneath Mount Zhongnan. Where the rope breaks is the place of my burial — you must not err. If you go against my words, I shall not rest at peace." Hearing the master's words, Qiu and Liu and the others choked and wished to weep. Master Chongyang said, "Do not work yourselves up into this child's mood!" Though the master directed them so, Qiu, Liu, and the others could but harbor sorrow and give rise to grief — of this there is no need to speak.
At noon the next day the master, in well-ordered dress, sat upright upon his rush cushion, called the six, Qiu, Liu, Tan, Ma, Hao, and Wang, near, and expounded the Way:

The method of cultivating together nature and lifespan requires both the outer and the inner. If the outer merit is lacking, the virtuous nature is incomplete; if the inner merit is lacking, the source and root are not clear.

As for the outer merit: throughout one's life, in all one's inward bearing, one must see to it there is no shortfall. Each word must be guarded — words have their merit; each act must be careful — acts have their merit. Each matter must not be careless; even a single trifle (meaning the smallest quantity, e.g., a single act of kindness) must be held strict about. There is nothing that is not the accumulation of merit, the advancing of merit.

What then is the inner merit? Watchfulness should not sink into dullness; guard the intent as one guards a city's danger. In blankness, alight on not a single thing; guard the mind more strictly than one guards the body. At times the heavenly and the human stand a hair apart (differing by the merest fraction), and that hair's breadth is where they do battle.

Let me set the inner merit forth with emphasis. The inner merit cannot be seen in form, cannot be sought in appearance, cannot be had by luck, cannot be gotten by slack ease. Sweep away a hair's worth of form and there is a hair's worth of yang as master; sweep away countless forms and there is countless yang born. Sweep the forms utterly clean, leaving not the least (a speck of) taint, and it is the body of pure yang.

There are some cultivators of the Way who are not lacking a firm faith, but whose fault lies in wanting quick success: before the work is done, they think of attaining the fruit. There are others who practice my Way who do not fail to apply their care, but whose fault lies in indolent ease: day after day they drowse as if to sleep, hour after hour depressed and joyless; their spirit lacks vigor, they find it hard to carry on the practice, and will not apply themselves. Do they not know that even a single skill and a single craft requires exhausting the mind's boundless contrivance before it can be used at will; even a half-thread and a half-silk requires spending a great deal of effort before it satisfies the heart? How then can those who would learn to be immortals fail to undergo bitter toil?

When Master Chongyang had finished, he took a book, named the Collected Works of Concealment of Light. It was written by his own hand, and within it were the way of concealing one's traces and the wonder of withdrawing into seclusion. He gave it to Ma Danyang and said, "You six should search its pages for the ultimate principle. To know it is not hard; to practice it is hard. Make sure you strive to practice it, and do not betray my heart. Your fellow practitioner Sun has a fruit of the Way nearly ripe; give him no more thought. Only Qiu Changchun has too few merits and practices; you should guide him a little. Liu Changsheng has not yet emptied his forms of appearance, and another wave of troubles awaits him. Hao Taigu, going east and returning west, the place he sees is the place where he concludes the Way. Tan Changzhen, meeting a Gu, will penetrate the mystery. Wang Yuyang, meeting a Yao, will enter the subtle. Qiu Changchun, by the edge of the Panshi stream the bitter root is exhausted; at the Dragon-flying gate the great elixir is complete." When Master Chongyang had spoken, he smiled and passed away.

Qiu, Liu, and the others reverently obeyed the master's last instructions, not daring to proclaim it abroad, and encoffined him according to the rite. They bound the coffin with ropes, found a carrying-pole and two cross-bars. The next morning Qiu, Wang, Tan, and Hao — four of them — shouldered the coffin and set off. Liu Changsheng carried the luggage behind. Ma Danyang saw them on their way more than twenty li; when they parted, he took from his side a pouch of small broken silver, about forty or fifty taels, and gave it to Liu Changsheng, saying, "The silver of the household was spent by the master in good works, so I could not raise more at once. Take this little broken silver as traveling money; if you are frugal on the road it will be enough. After you have buried the master, come back quickly, and we, fellow practitioners of the same school, will cultivate together in one place." Liu Changsheng took the silver and parted from Danyang. They had not gone a few li when they saw a crowd holding inch-long incense and scraps of paper, blocking the road with offerings. Liu Changsheng drew near and saw that they were all those false cultivators who had studied the Way among the master's disciples. Liu Changsheng thanked each in turn, but who would have thought — whereas during his life Master Chongyang could never abide false cultivators of the Way, now in death his true spirit did not sleep, and at the sight of them was still offended; from within the coffin it sent forth a blast of stench, so foul that everyone covered his nose, each retched, and could no longer stand upright. They knocked a few random head-bows and all went off, and the stench subsided.

Qiu Changchun and Hao Taigu and the others, bearing the coffin, went on westward. Before they had walked ten li, someone blocked the road and offered them a meal. Qiu and Liu and the others took it for someone who had known the master in former years, and who now, hearing the master had gone to heaven, had specially brought a meal to show a human kindness — no wonder. They quickly set down the coffin and came to eat. When they were done they said a word of thanks, shouldered the coffin again, and went on. Before long they saw an old temple by the roadside; no longer able to carry it, they set the coffin down on the flat ground and lodged in the temple that night. At daybreak the next day, having borne it to the time of breakfast, again someone blocked the road and served a meal. At lunchtime it was the same. When it was late they found a cold temple to put up in. So they went for more than a month and reached the border of Shaanxi. Qiu Changchun thought to himself, "Is this not strange! In all heaven and earth, how could such a coincidence happen? Nearby, one might suppose it was someone known to the master, doing a kindness; that is not beyond reckoning. But now after so great a distance, still someone blocks the road to offer a meal — the matter is truly extraordinary." He was musing to himself when, at noon, someone brought a meal and asked them to eat. Liu, Hao, Wang, and Tan thanked the man and took up bowls and chopsticks to eat. Qiu Changchun pulled the bearer aside and asked, "How did you know we would come here? And what is your reason for bringing us this meal?" The bearer said, "This morning an old Taoist in a yellow robe came begging alms in our village and said, 'I have five disciples bringing a coffin from Shandong, and they will pass this way; they wish to trouble some household for a meal.' My master is the most charitable, and hearing this he sent me with this meal."

Changchun took this to heart. The next morning, at the time of breakfast, he pretended his belly ached and said he had to go to the village ahead to beg a bowl of hot soup. He asked Liu Changsheng to help carry a share. Changsheng agreed, handed him the luggage, took up the pole, and shouldered the coffin. Qiu Changchun, carrying the luggage on his back, strode ahead several li and indeed saw an old man in a yellow Taoist robe, bearing something like the master's countenance, going into the village ahead. Qiu Changchun hurried a few steps, caught up, seized the robe with one hand, knelt down, and cried, "Master, go slowly — your disciple is here waiting upon you." Master Chongyang turned around, his face full of anger, and scolded Changchun, "You sin-making disciple! You do not know the way of the fullness and emptiness of heaven and earth, of the waxing and waning and the concealing of traces. You only show your cleverness and let slip the immortals' secret. Judging from this, you will have to spend yet another three years at the work of subduing demons — you bring this on yourself." So saying, he turned into a clear wind and was gone.

Changchun was in the midst of his remorse when he saw the coffin come up; he hurried to take the pole and shoulder it, and gave the luggage back to Changsheng. From then on, no one ever again brought a meal. Had it not been for the silver Ma Danyang had given them as traveling money, they could hardly have escaped starving.

After half a month more they reached Zhongnan. Suddenly their ropes all broke at once and the coffin fell to the ground. Changchun looked, and saw an old man standing at the head of the village before them; he went up and made a bow. Before the words left his mouth, the old man asked, "Are you the ones who have carried a coffin back from Shandong?" Qiu Changchun answered, "Just so. How did you know, uncle?" The old man said, "Last night I dreamed of Wang the successful candidate, who said he was dead. Five disciples bore his coffin from Shandong to this place, and begged me to give a plot of ground to bury him. I thought how in old days I sat the provincial examination with him in the provincial capital, and the two of us were great friends, so I agreed readily. I asked him when he was to be buried, and he said at noon today. I woke and knew it was a dream, half-believing and half-doubting, and came out to look several times, and only now see you bearing the coffin, which has just come to rest on this old man's land." Changchun then told the old man the master's words, that where the rope breaks is the place of his burial. The old man was much pleased, and went in to call out a few farmhands, each with a digging-spade and basket, and they came to the coffin. They moved the coffin over, dug a shaft at that place, and buried it, and in a moment raised a great mound. Qiu, Liu, and the others bowed thanks to the old man and thanked the farmhands for their pains. The old man then invited the brothers into the village and entertained them to a vegetarian meal. Thereupon Qiu, Liu, and the rest took leave of the old man, and having asked the way to the village of Daxiao, made a bow and went. What came of this journey? Listen to the next chapter for the answer.
